newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada says to do much better than deficit goal.
newsitem.headline: Canada says to do much better than deficit goal.

text.p: Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Tuesday the federal government would do much better than its C$19 billion deficit target for 1996-97.

"It's quite clear that we're going to do better than the 19 (billion) that was set out. That's very good news. But we haven't got all the large numbers in yet, and as you know every year, if you look back, every year there have been adjustments of anywhere from C$4 to C$6 billion. So I think we'll have to wait for the final numbers," Martin said.
"We're doing much better because interest rates are down. They're lower than what had been projected," he added.
The Finance Department on Monday reported a deficit for the first 11 months of the fiscal year -- April 1996 through February 1997 -- of C$7.83 billion, compared with C$23.28 billion a year earlier.
The C$4 billion to C$6 billion of possible extra charges that Martin referred to are end-of-year adjustments.

But clearly even if C$6 billion were added to C$7.83 billion -- along with the deficit for March 1997 which is to be announced next month -- the total is likely to be well under the C$19 billion target Martin had set. That itself is a downward revision from an original goal of C$24.3 billion.

Asked why he would now go through with planned spending cuts, Martin referred to the risk of losing the gains from lower interest rates which has enabled the deficit to come in so much lower than budgeted.
"A great deal of that is the confidence in our fiscal discipline, and I don't think anybody would expect us to give up on that fiscal discipline at this stage," he told reporters.

Questioned on whether this would give the government money to spend on things like job creation as it goes into a general election campaign -- expected to start in late April -- he said: "No, we've basically set out our numbers, and we've established in the budget our priorities, and we're going to stay with that."
He said those lower interest rates had been responsible for creating jobs.
